clue.text: Old show using a "them and us" trope reinvented

indicators.note: something reinvented is remade in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A long-running production built around a them-and-us theme is given a fresh treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'and' inside the quoted phrase is only a joining word, not part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's play has run in London's West End since 1952, so it is a very old show.

clue.text: Pieces of ephemera heaped around old ladies' rooms

indicators.note: around means the run of letters is turned the other way, read right to left
the answer is made from pieces of the letters of these two words, running across them

explanation.surface: Bits of collectable paper junk are piled up in the rooms of elderly women.
explanation.walkthrough: Read EPHEMERAHEAPED right to left and the run HAREM appears across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the women's quarters in a traditional Muslim household; 'old' points to the historical sense.

clue.text: Show your backside — though I never do

definitions.text: Show your backside — though I never do

parts.words: Show your backside — though I never do
parts.note: to show your bare bottom is a slang verb; the speaker is the heavenly body that always keeps one face towards Earth, so never shows its far side

explanation.walkthrough: The verb meaning to bare your bottom is also the name of the satellite that is tidally locked, so its far side is never seen from Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Mooning is slang for baring your buttocks, and Earth's satellite never turns its far side to us.

clue.text: Article in Le Monde leads to secret agents feeling extremely exposed

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article, as would appear in the French paper Le Monde

indicators.note: the leads, or front letters, of each of the following four words are taken

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about undercover spies leaves them feeling very vulnerable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Le Monde' is a French newspaper, which tells you the article is a French one.
explanation.definitionFit: Being exposed means being open to danger, without protection or cover.

clue.text: Far from popular CEO tries to mingle

indicators.note: letters that mingle mix together, so these are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An unpopular chief executive makes an effort to socialise with staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Something esoteric appeals only to a small circle of insiders, the opposite of having mass appeal.

clue.text: European people bringing down current wise guy

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing a letter down moves it lower, from the top to the bottom

parts.note: the Irish are a European people
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Europeans topple a clever man in power, a nod to the Conservative leadership contest of 2022.
explanation.walkthrough: The I at the front of IRISH is moved to the end, giving RISHI.
explanation.definitionFit: A rishi is a Hindu sage or holy seer, so a wise man; the surface also hints at Rishi Sunak.

clue.text: Salesperson breaks verbal contract made up for customers

indicators.note: the salesperson breaks into the word, sitting inside it
verbal means spoken, so the word is heard aloud and spelt as its sound-alike

parts.note: a pact is a contract or agreement
a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: A sales rep breaks a spoken agreement he invented to please clients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Verbal contract' looks like one idea, an oral deal; in fact 'verbal' tells you to hear PACT aloud as PACKED.
explanation.definitionFit: Prepacked goods are wrapped and made up in advance, ready for sale to shoppers.

clue.text: Tailless breed crossed with mongrels to make pointers

indicators.note: one word is crossed into the other, sitting inside it

parts.note: curs are mongrel dogs

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a sort is a kind or breed

explanation.surface: Breeding a dog without a tail with some mongrels to produce pointer dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointers' looks like a breed of gundog, fitting the dog-breeding scene; it means the on-screen arrows.
explanation.definitionFit: Cursors are the movable markers on a computer screen that show where you are pointing.

clue.text: Good thing Pussy and agent Bond changed a bit right before the end

parts.note: a pussy is a cat
a spy is a secret agent

indicators.text: changed a bit right before the end
indicators.note: the letter just before the final one is changed to a different letter, here the A of the clue

parts.note: James Bond, the fictional agent

explanation.surface: A cat and James Bond get a small change just before the finale.
explanation.walkthrough: JAMES has its second-last letter E changed to A, making JAMAS; 'a bit' supplies the new letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: The cat's pyjamas is an old idiom, like the bee's knees, for something excellent.

clue.text: Exotic stores containing unknown seafood

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the unknown inside them
exotic means strange or unusual, so the letters are put into a strange order

parts.note: y is one of the algebra letters used for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: Unusual shops stock an unidentified kind of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Oysters are shellfish eaten raw or cooked, a classic example of seafood.

clue.text: Your setter's not above rejigging past clue, which is risky

indicators.note: in a down entry, not above means below, so this piece comes after
rejigging means rearranging, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
the setter speaking would say I have, shortened to I've

explanation.surface: The setter admits to reworking an old clue, which is a gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not above' looks like a boast of humility; in a down entry it places I'VE below the anagram of PAST CLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A speculative venture is one undertaken on chance with no guarantee of success, hence hazardous.

clue.text: See 26
Sturgeon caught with line and later skinned for camp?

indicators.note: caught means heard, so FM is spelt out the way it sounds when said

parts.note: Nicola Sturgeon was Scotland's First Minister, FM for short

indicators.note: skinned means the outer letters are stripped from each word, leaving the middles

explanation.surface: A sturgeon is landed on a fishing line and then has its skin removed, posed as a riddle about camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sturgeon caught with line' reads like fishing, but Sturgeon is the politician, and 'caught' means heard: F M said aloud is EFF EM. Then line and later lose their ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp is an adjective for exaggerated, affected mannerisms, often linked with being unmanly.

clue.text: Straighten out joint with doctor

parts.note: co- is the prefix meaning joint or together, as in co-owner
MB is a medical degree, Bachelor of Medicine, so a doctor

explanation.surface: Fixing a dislocated joint with a doctor's help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straighten out' plus 'joint' and 'doctor' suggests setting a limb; the answer is what you do to tangled hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Combing hair untangles it and makes it smooth and neat.

clue.text: Garden area quiet when the news comes on

parts.note: p is the musical marking piano, meaning quiet
the news is on at ten, written AT 10, and 10 read as letters is IO

explanation.surface: The garden falls silent when the evening news begins.
explanation.walkthrough: This refers to the ITV programme News at Ten; the figures 10 are read as the letters I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A patio is a paved outdoor space next to a house, used for sitting out.

clue.text: Time machine pulling in three different directions is late arriving

indicators.note: the time machine pulls the letters in, so they sit inside it

parts.note: the TARDIS is the time machine in the TV series Doctor Who
north, east and south are three compass points

explanation.surface: Doctor Who's ship, dragged three ways at once, turns up behind schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardiness is the fault of being late, so a noun for a late arrival or lateness.

clue.text: Tim Burton's first film for kids introduces this country to initially remote city

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the country is introduced, brought in between the two opening letters
first here asks for just the opening letter of the director's surname
initially means only the opening letter of the little word to is kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: the setter writes from the United Kingdom
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, fit for children

explanation.surface: A Tim Burton family film introduces Britain to a faraway place.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British censors' rating for films suitable for all, including children. The setter's ordering is loose: UK is brought in between B and T, and the film's U ends the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Timbuktu, in Mali, is proverbial for being the most far-flung place imaginable.

clue.text: Crash the baby shower

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the swollen belly that shows a baby is on the way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Baby shower' reads as the party for a mother-to-be; split it as 'shower' meaning one who shows, and it becomes the pregnant belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A small collision is a bump, and a pregnant woman's rounded stomach is also called a bump.

clue.text: Heir's beginning song and dance that might make Queen cough up

definitions.text: that might make Queen cough up

indicators.note: beginning points to the opening letter of the word

parts.note: an air is a tune or song
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: The heir to the throne's early singing and dancing so irritates the monarch she coughs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' looks royal, fitting 'Heir'; here it is a female cat, which coughs up fur swallowed while grooming.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairball is a wad of swallowed fur that a cat brings up, and a queen is a female cat.

clue.text: Naked baby boomers start to jive around — Methuselah's even more bubbly than this

definitions.text: Methuselah's even more bubbly than this

indicators.note: the start of the word, its first letter, is taken
the letters are moved around into a new order
stripped bare of their outer letters, so both words lose their first and last letters

explanation.surface: Nude baby boomers begin dancing, and the setter claims to be more sparkling than they are.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is both the setter's name and a champagne bottle size larger than this one, so it holds more bubbly. The jive letter leads, ahead of the rearranged middles.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeroboam is a large champagne bottle, usually four standard bottles, smaller than a methuselah of eight.

clue.text: See 22
Sort of emissions vehicle cap cut by 50%

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: half of the word's letters are cut away, leaving the first half

parts.note: a bonnet is a kind of cap or soft hat

explanation.surface: A plan to halve the cap on car emissions.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbon emissions are the carbon dioxide released by burning fuel, a common descriptor of pollution.

clue.text: American made a minister, somehow circumventing the usual channels?

indicators.note: somehow means in some unexplained way, so the letters are arranged afresh

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American is given a ministerial post by bypassing the normal procedures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circumventing' only links here: the American's letters are put in among the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Mainstream media are the established newspapers and broadcasters, the conventional outlets of news.

clue.text: Finalists in lawless melee recalled extreme fight

indicators.note: the finalists of these words are their last letters
recalled means called back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: OTT, over the top, means extreme

explanation.surface: The last competitors left in a lawless brawl remember an especially vicious bout.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is a brief but vigorous argument or scuffle.

clue.text: German vehicle would be sound if it had a wheel

indicators.note: the answer would become the other word, so the two differ by one piece
the answer lacks the piece, so the longer word has it taken away

parts.note: audio means sound, as in audio equipment
a wheel is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A German car would be safe if only it had a wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like sound in the sense of safe or roadworthy; it means audio. Take away the O and the German car maker is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Audi is the German car manufacturer, so one of its cars is a German vehicle.

clue.text: Someone telling you where to go's a woman after my own heart

definitions.text: Someone telling you where to go

indicators.note: after places the woman following the setter's heart in the answer

parts.note: the setter is Methuselah, and the heart of that name is the middle pair of letters
her is a pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: Someone bossing you about is a woman just like me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A woman after my own heart' is an idiom for a kindred spirit; here 'my own' is the setter, Methuselah, whose name has its heart in the fifth and sixth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An usher shows people to their seats in a theatre or church, so directs them.

clue.text: Period drama with parts in wrong order creates a gap in education

indicators.note: the two pieces are placed the other way round from the clue's order

parts.note: a play is a drama
time is a period

explanation.surface: A historical costume drama whose scenes are shuffled leaves a hole in someone's schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Period drama' reads as one thing, a costume drama; split it into its two words and swap them.
explanation.definitionFit: Playtime is the break between lessons at school, a gap in the teaching day.

clue.text: Disrespect Radiohead's In Rainbows? On the contrary!

indicators.note: the answer is in the run of letters of the clue's opening words
the reverse of what is asked: not the words in Rainbows, but rainbows in the words

explanation.surface: Is it disrespectful to Radiohead to mention their album In Rainbows? Quite the reverse!
explanation.walkthrough: In Rainbows is a 2007 Radiohead album. The question says the words are inside rainbows; 'On the contrary' flips it, so rainbows are inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectra, plural of spectrum, are bands of coloured light, which is what rainbows are.

clue.text: Awkward fling gotten over with short ones

indicators.note: turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to lob is to fling or throw

indicators.note: short means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: ones stands in for flings again: shies are throws

explanation.surface: A clumsy affair is put behind someone, with some brief ones too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ones' points back to 'fling', so it means more flings, SHIES, then cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolshie is British slang for awkward and uncooperative, from Bolshevik.

clue.text: Recon specialist ditching uniform and ID holder outside Germany's police HQ

indicators.note: ditching means dropping, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: a scout is sent ahead for reconnaissance
Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the lanyard goes outside the letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a lanyard is a cord worn round the neck that holds an ID badge
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: A reconnaissance expert takes off his uniform and badge cord outside German police headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Germany's police HQ' suggests a German force, but Germany only supplies its vehicle code; the answer is London's Metropolitan Police headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police, and a byword for the force itself.
